title: When a webhook uses an HMAC-over-raw-body signature, verify the raw bytes before parsing
summary: When an inbound webhook authenticates senders with an HMAC/shared-secret signature computed over the raw request body, an agent that calls request.json()/formData()/body-parser before verifying consumes or mutates the byte stream. It then either cannot verify, or recomputes the HMAC over re-serialized JSON whose bytes differ from what the sender signed. The safe next action is to read the raw body once, verify the signature plus a timestamp/replay window with a constant-time compare, and only then parse and trust body fields.
ai_value: Stops agents from shipping webhook endpoints that silently accept forged or replayed deliveries, fail verification against the real signing string, leak the digest through a non-constant-time compare, or act on tenant/account fields from an unverified body. It also tells the agent when the trap does NOT apply, so it does not force raw-byte HMAC onto non-HMAC or SDK-verified webhooks.

contexts: implementing an inbound HTTP webhook or callback endpoint that authenticates senders via an HMAC or shared-secret signature header over the request body
a web framework or middleware parses the request body (JSON, form, multipart) or runs schema validation before the route handler
the provider documents a signing string over the raw bytes plus a timestamp or nonce (for example {timestamp}.{body} or v0:{timestamp}:{body})
the request body carries tenant, account, user, or integration identifiers that the handler will act on
adapting a provider-neutral webhook template before a specific provider's signature contract is finalized

trigger_signals.description: The body is parsed (json(), formData(), express.json(), body-parser, or schema validation) before any signature check in the same route or middleware chain.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The raw byte stream is consumed or normalized before verification, so verification will be impossible or run over the wrong bytes. Reorder to verify first.

trigger_signals.description: The HMAC input is built from re-serialized parsed data instead of the exact received bytes.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Re-serialization changes whitespace, key order, or encoding, so the signed bytes differ from JSON.stringify(parsed). Verification is invalid even if a self-signed test passes.

trigger_signals.description: A tenant, account, user, or integration identifier is read from the body, query, or header before verification succeeds.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Attacker-controlled fields are driving authorization or data writes before authentication. Parse and trust fields only after verification.

trigger_signals.description: The signature covers only the body; there is no timestamp, nonce, or delivery-id binding and no freshness window check.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The endpoint is replayable: a captured valid delivery can be resent indefinitely. Bind and check a timestamp/nonce.

trigger_signals.description: The signature is compared with ==, ===, or string equality on the digest.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Byte-by-byte short-circuit comparison leaks the digest through timing. Use a constant-time compare after length and format checks.

trigger_signals.description: Tests sign one happy-path fixture only; there are no malformed, missing-header, stale-timestamp, or replay assertions.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The security-relevant paths are the negative ones and are unverified. Add negative-path tests before trusting the endpoint.

negative_signals.description: A maintained provider SDK or framework binding already captures the raw body and verifies the signature before the handler runs (for example a construct-event helper).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The raw-body-before-parse obligation is already met upstream. Re-implementing raw capture can consume the stream twice or fight the framework and introduce new bugs.

negative_signals.description: The provider's documented signature scheme is computed over a canonicalized or constructed representation of selected fields, not the literal received bytes (for example a signed string-to-sign or a SHA256 over a constructed message; AWS SNS is one such scheme).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Raw-byte verification would wrongly fail. Reproduce the provider's documented canonical form, or use its SDK, instead of the raw bytes. Raw-body-before-parse is not provider-universal.

negative_signals.description: The endpoint's authentication is transport- or token-based: mutual TLS, an asymmetric/public-key-verified JWT/JWS, or an IP allow-list on a trusted internal-only network, with no shared-secret body HMAC.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: There is no body-HMAC signing string to verify; the trap is out of scope and different verification rules apply.

negative_signals.description: No shared secret or signing scheme exists between sender and receiver (for example an unsigned internal event bus protected by separate access control).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: This trap does not apply; do not invent a signature requirement where the contract has none.

negative_signals.description: The handler is read-only/idempotent and takes no privileged action or data write from body fields.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The forgery/replay harm model (acting on unverified fields) is bounded. Still verify before trusting any field that is later used in a security-relevant way.

common_wrong_assumptions: I can parse the JSON first and then verify the signature over the parsed object.
Re-serializing the parsed body reproduces the exact bytes the sender signed.
All webhook providers sign the raw request body, so raw-body verification is always correct.
The HMAC is over just the body, so I do not need the timestamp.
Idempotency or delivery-id dedupe is the same as replay protection.
A plain ==/=== comparison on the hex digest is fine.
A passing happy-path test means verification is correct.
Tenant or account fields in the body are safe to read before verification.

first_checks.check: Read the route handler and middleware registration top to bottom; confirm the raw body is captured and the signature plus timestamp are verified before any parse, schema validation, or service call.
first_checks.why: Ordering is the root cause: parsing first consumes or normalizes the bytes that must be verified.

first_checks.check: Confirm the provider's signature contract: is it an HMAC/shared-secret over the raw body, a canonicalized string-to-sign, or non-HMAC transport auth?
first_checks.why: The trap only applies to HMAC-over-raw-body schemes. Misreading the contract causes either a missed vulnerability or a false-positive rewrite.
files: existing verification code or SDK usage

first_checks.check: If HMAC-over-raw-body: confirm the HMAC input is the exact received bytes matched to the documented signing string, not JSON.stringify(parsed).
first_checks.why: Whitespace, key order, and encoding differences in re-serialized JSON break verification.

first_checks.check: Confirm a timestamp or nonce is bound into the signature and a bounded freshness window (commonly a few minutes) is enforced, and that comparison is constant-time after length/format checks.
first_checks.why: Without a freshness window valid deliveries are replayable; string equality on the digest leaks it via timing.

first_checks.check: Confirm tests cover bad signature, missing signature/timestamp header, stale timestamp, success, and replay, not just one happy fixture.
first_checks.why: The negative paths are the security-relevant ones and are usually the unverified gaps.

decision_rules.condition: The provider contract is an HMAC/shared-secret signature over the raw body, and the body is parsed before signature verification in the handler or middleware chain.
decision_rules.then: Capture the raw body once (size-capped), verify the signature and timestamp, then parse. In Express, register the raw/verify route before express.json() or retain the buffer via a body-parser verify hook.

decision_rules.condition: The HMAC is computed over re-serialized or parsed data instead of the received bytes.
decision_rules.then: Build the HMAC input from the exact received bytes following the provider's documented signing string (for example {timestamp}.{body} or v0:{timestamp}:{body}).

decision_rules.condition: The signature is the only signed element and there is no freshness/replay check.
decision_rules.then: Verify the timestamp is part of the signed string and reject deliveries outside a bounded window; do not rely on idempotency alone for replay protection.

decision_rules.condition: The digest is compared with ==/===/string equality.
decision_rules.then: Replace with a constant-time compare (for example crypto.timingSafeEqual, hmac.compare_digest, or secure_compare) after length and format checks.

decision_rules.condition: A provider SDK already returns a verified raw body, or the scheme signs canonicalized/constructed content, or authentication is mTLS/asymmetric/internal-trusted with no body HMAC.
decision_rules.then: This trap does not apply. Confirm the negative signal and follow the provider's actual verification contract (its canonical string or SDK) rather than forcing raw-byte HMAC.

decision_rules.condition: Tenant/account/source fields are read or acted on before verification passes.
decision_rules.then: Treat as a security-sensitive change: do not auto-apply. Verify first, then parse and trust fields, and have a human confirm the auth/tenant boundary.

do_not: Do not verify a signature over re-serialized/parsed JSON instead of the received bytes.
Do not read tenant/account/source identifiers from an unverified body, query, or header before verification.
Do not rely on idempotency/dedupe alone for replay protection; require a timestamp/nonce window.
Do not compare digests with ==/===/string equality.
Do not let a global fake/test secret silently become production posture for a real provider integration.
Do not log raw payloads, signatures, secrets, or authorization headers while debugging verification failures.
Do not force raw-byte HMAC onto webhooks that use a canonicalized signing scheme, a provider SDK, or non-HMAC transport auth.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Identify the provider's signature contract first. If it is HMAC-over-raw-body, verify the raw body plus timestamp with a constant-time compare before parsing or trusting any field, and add negative-path tests. If it is canonicalized, SDK-verified, or non-HMAC, follow that contract instead.

risk.notes: Touches authentication, authorization, and trust boundaries: a wrong change can silently accept forged or replayed webhooks or break legitimate delivery processing. The exact signing string, tolerance window, secret lookup, replay store, and response codes must follow each real provider's contract. This record guides diagnosis and verify-before-parse ordering; it does not authorize disabling verification or relaxing a window in production.

sources.excerpt: The hash signature will appear in each delivery as the value of the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. ... Never use a plain == operator. Instead consider using a method like secure_compare or crypto.timingSafeEqual, which performs a 'constant time' string comparison to help mitigate certain timing attacks against regular equality operators. ... Make sure that the payload and headers are not modified before verification.
sources.supports: Official source for the HMAC-SHA256 signature header, the explicit requirement to use a constant-time comparison rather than ==, and the rule that the payload must not be modified before verification.

sources.excerpt: Use the raw request body, without headers, before it has been deserialized from JSON or other forms. ... Concatenate the version number, the timestamp, and the request body together, using a colon (:) as a delimiter. ... The signature depends on the timestamp to protect against replay attacks. ... For best practice, use an hmac compare function instead of directly comparing the signatures for equality.
sources.supports: Second independent provider confirming raw-body-before-deserialization, a {version}:{timestamp}:{body} signing string, timestamp-bound replay protection, and constant-time hmac comparison.

sources.excerpt: To ensure message integrity and prevent spoofing, you must verify the signature before processing any Amazon SNS messages. ... SignatureVersion2 - Uses an SHA256 hash of the message. ... The AWS SDKs for Amazon SNS provide built-in validation logic, reducing the risk of misimplementation. ... Reject any message with an unexpected TopicArn to prevent spoofing.
sources.supports: Counterexample grounding the negative signal: a provider whose signature is computed over a constructed representation of the message (with SDK-provided validation), not an HMAC over the raw HTTP request body, so raw-body-before-parse is not provider-universal.
